The Court made the following:
Judgment:

-
Challenge in this M.A.C.M.A is to the award dated 24.08.2016 in O.P.No.99 of 2014, on the file of the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal-cum-VI Additional District Judge, Ananthapur at Gooty,
("Tribunal" for short) whereunder, the Tribunal dealing with a claim for compensation with regard to the injuries sustained by the injured in a motor vehicle accident occurred on 28.03.2013 at 11.30 am, as against the original claim of Rs.4,00,000/- awarded a sum of Rs.2,50,000/- towards the compensation.
2. The parties to this M.A.C.M.A will hereinafter be referred to as described before the Tribunal for the sake of convenience.
3. The case of the petitioner in the O.P.No.99 of 2014 according to the petition averments, in brief, is that:
The injured petitioner was 53 years old hale and healthy person used to earn Rs.6,000/- per month by doing cultivation.
All his family members were depending upon his earnings.
On 28.03.2013 petitioner purchased two bulls at Dhone bullocks fair.
Petitioner and others who also purchased bullocks at that fair engaged Bolero trolley vehicle bearing No.AP02TA7336 on hire basis for transporting their purchased bulls from Dhone to Gooty Town.

When said vehicle passed Pothudoddi Village of Peapully Mandal on N.H.44 Road at about 11.30 am, its driver had driven it in a rash and negligent manner with high speed and unable to control the said vehicle.
Consequently, said vehicle dashed the road dividers and turtle.
Petitioners and others who were travelling along with their respective bulls in that vehicle received injuries.
Immediately they were shifted to Government Hospital, Gooty for medical treatment in 108 Ambulance.
Petitioner sustained fracture of left leg, both bones, right leg foot, right hand wrist and multiple simple injuries all over the body.
He took treatment at Pavani, YSR and Anantapur Orthopedic Centre, Anantapuramu and he incurred a sum of Rs.1,00,000/- for medical, hospital and other expenses.
Now petitioner became partial permanent disabled person.
Due to said accident he could not lift heavy weights and he is not able to sit and squat normally and he lost his earnings.

The accident was occurred solely due to rash and negligent driving of the driver of said Bolero Vehicle and a case was registered in Cr.No.22/2013 u/s 337 and 338 IPC at Peapully P.S. against the driver of said Bolero Vehicle.

1st respondent being the owner-cum-insured, 2nd respondent being insurer and 3rd respondent being the driver of said vehicle are jointly and severally liable to pay the compensation of Rs.4,00,000/- to the petitioner with interest at 12% per annum from the date of the petition till the date of realization.
4. The 1st respondent and 3rd respondent remained ex-parte.

2 5. The 2nd respondent got filed a counter opposing the prayer and contending in substance that the petitioner was taking his bulls along with him in the crime vehicle.
So he was not eligible to claim compensation on the ground that he was owner.
The bulls which were transported do not come under the description of goods under Section 2 (13) of M.V. Act, 1988.
The injured was unauthorized passenger in the offending lorry which is a goods vehicle.
As many as ten persons boarded the offending vehicle individually claiming to be the owner of the goods by purchasing one bull each travelled.
No premium is paid to the owner of bulls.
Hence, no liability can be fixed.
There will be one owner of the goods.
The petitioner did not prove that he travelled as owner, in the absence of the same, claim is not maintainable.
Hence, the claim is to be dismissed.

6. On the basis of the above pleadings, the Tribunal settled the following issues for trial:
(1) Whether the road accident was occurred on 28.03.2013 at about 11.30 am on N.H.44 road after passing Pothudoddi Village, Peapully Mandal, Kurnool District due to rash and negligent driving of Bolero Trolley bearing No.AP02TA7336 by its driver as alleged by the petitioner?
( 2) Whether the petitioner is entitled to claim compensation?
If so, to what amount and from whom?

(3) To what relief?
7.
During the course of enquiry, on behalf of the petitioners, P.W.1 to P.W.3 were examined.
Exs.A1 to A7 were marked.
On behalf of the respondents, R.W.1 to R.W.3 were examined and Exs.B.1 and B2 and Exs.X1 to X3 were marked.

8. The Tribunal on hearing both sides and on considering the oral as well as documentary evidence held that the accident occurred was on account of rash and negligent driving made by the driver of offending vehicle.
The Tribunal further negatived the contention of the contesting respondent that bulls do not come under the purview of the goods under M.V. Act.

The Tribunal looking into the evidence of R.W.1 and admissions made was of the view that driver of the offending vehicle had a valid driving license and further in view of the terms under Ex.B1, company is liable to pay the compensation for the injuries caused to the owner of the bulls.

While holding so, the Tribunal awarded a sum of Rs.2,50,000/- as compensation and directed the 2nd respondent to pay the compensation and later to recover the same from the owner of the offending vehicle.

The unsuccessful 2nd respondent/insurance company felt aggrieved of the award filed the present M.A.C.M.A.
9.

Now, in deciding the M.A.C.M.A., the point that arises for determination is as follows:
Whether the award dated 24.08.2016 in O.P.No.99 of 2014, on the file of the Chairman, Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal-cum-VI Additional District Judge,
Ananthapur at Gooty, is sustainable under law and facts and whether there are any other grounds to interfere with the same?

sentences.text: Point:

10. Sri Chekuri Sripathi Rao, learned counsel for the appellant, through video conference would contend that the bulls that were transported in the offending vehicle cannot come under the purview of goods under Section 2 (13) of M.V. Act, 1988.
The insurer did not claim any premium to cover the risk of the passengers.
There was overloading of as many as ten persons who travelled in the offending vehicle claiming to be the owners of goods by purchasing bulls, as such there are policy violations.
The claimant was unauthorized passenger which the Tribunal failed to look into.
There were policy violations which the Tribunal did not consider.

The direction of the Tribunal to the appellant/respondent No.2 to pay the amount first and to recover the same is not sustainable and the responsibility can be fixed on respondent Nos.1 and 3 alone to pay the compensation and the appellant may be absolved.

11. Learned counsel for the 1st respondent/claimant would contend that the Tribunal on overall appreciation of the evidence ordered the 2nd respondent to pay the compensation and to recover the same from the 1st respondent as such the award needs no interference.
12.

Insofar as the finding of the Tribunal that the accident occurred was due to rash and negligent driving of the driver of the offending vehicle is concerned, it is not sought to be disturbed in the present MACMA.
Apart from this P.W.1 who was the injured in his chief examination put forth the facts in tune with the pleadings.
Through his chief examination Exs.A1 to A7 were marked.
Ex. A1
was the attested Xerox copy of FIR.
Ex . A2
was the attested Xerox copy of wound certificate.
Ex . A3
was the attested Xerox copy of Charge sheet.
Ex . A4
was the physically disable certificate.
Ex . A5
was the bunch of medical bills prescriptions and reports.
Ex . A6
was the original medical bills.
Ex . A7
was the X-rays.
Further, the claimant examined P.W.2 and P.W.3 to speak of the injuries.

The evidence on record coupled with the outcome of the investigation pertaining to the FIR registered would show that the accident occurred was due to rash and negligent act of the 1st respondent in driving the offending vehicle.
13. The manner in which the Tribunal arrived at the compensation of Rs.2,50,000/- is not sought to be disturbed in the grounds of the Appeal.

So the substance of the contentions of the appellant is that the livestock cannot be considered as goods and further, the petitioner was unauthorized passenger who has no right to travel in the vehicle, as such fixing up the responsibility against the appellant is not sustainable.

14. It is to be noted that before the Tribunal, learned counsel for the petitioner relied upon a decision of erstwhile High Court of Andhra Pradesh in Bajaj Allianz General Insurance Co. Limited.,
Yerawada, Pune Vs. B.Hanumantha Reddy and another 1 it was observed as follows:
"In the instant case also, the insurance policy being package policy and the claimant having purchased the bull in the shandy, was travelling in the said van at relevant time, he being the owner of the goods cannot be treated as gratuitous passenger in the said vehicle and the learned Tribunal in my view rightly held that the appellant/insurance company is liable to pay compensation to him.

15. So, the Tribunal based on the above came to a conclusion that the bulls would come under the purview of Section 2(13) of the M.V. Act,1988.
16.

Coming to the contention of the appellant that the injured was unauthorized passenger, the evidence of P.W.1 in cross examination shows that along with him six bulls and five persons were there in the offending vehicle and the vehicle is a small jeep with an open body on the back side.
He denied that he was travelling in the vehicle as passenger by paying charges.
17. Ultimately, the vehicle was a small one with open space in the back side.

As seen from the evidence of R.W.1 who was representative of the insurance company in cross examination, he testified that a sum of Rs.75/- was collected towards non fare paying passengers and that IMT-37A is made for the legal liability to non fare paying passengers who are not employees of the insured covered under the proviso as per Ex.B1 policy and the company is liable to pay the compensation for the injuries caused to the owner of the bulls.
According to the admissions of R.W.1, amount was collected towards non fare paying passengers who can be termed as the owner of the goods.
According to the evidence of P.W.5, five persons travelled along with bulls.
It is the bounden duty of the insurance company to elicit the seating capacity of 2013(2) ALD 416 the vehicle.
In the absence of the same, insurance company cannot repudiate to pay the amount to the claimant first and then to recover.
18. The contention of the insurance company before the Tribunal that the driver had no valid driving license was not at all substantiated.

However, the Tribunal found some policy violations because of excessive seating capacity and ultimately, following the decisions held that the 2 nd respondent can be directed to pay the amount and then to recover the same from the 1st respondent/owner.
The findings of the Tribunal arrived at on thorough appreciation of the evidence cannot be interfered with.
Hence, this Court does not find any reason to interfere with the findings of the Tribunal.
19. In the result, the M.A.C.M.A is dismissed, but under the circumstances without costs.
Consequently, miscellaneous applications pending, if any, shall stand closed.
